stances.claim: In economic controversies, courts must defer to the political branches absent a clear constitutional violation or GAD -- elected leaders are accountable to the electorate for economic decisions.
Human rights and liberty cases are the reverse: courts must strictly construe laws in favor of the people and against the government.
Tañada v. Angara (1997) correctly upheld WTO ratification using deferential interpretation -- whether globalization is wise is outside judicial inquiry.
Long-term investors need stable, consistent, and predictable jurisprudence -- courts should interfere only when contracts clearly violate the Constitution or show GAD.
The NAIA Terminal 3 voiding was correct -- a clear and specific violation of public bidding law, not a policy disagreement -- illustrating the proper limits of deferential interpretation.

notable_anecdotes: Tañada v. Angara (May 2, 1997): senators challenged WTO ratification on economic nationalism grounds; the SC unanimously upheld ratification using deferential interpretation -- one of the author's most frequently cited precedents.

FDR's New Deal court-packing plan: US SC blocked New Deal programs until Justice Owen Roberts joined the liberal bloc ('switch in time that saved nine') -- FDR desisted; the closest the US came to political capture of its SC.

NAIA Terminal 3 voiding: the SC as 'not an unwanted interloper' when it enforces the law on public bidding -- the 'level the playing field' principle as the boundary case of permissible judicial economic intervention.

one_paragraph_summary: Against the backdrop of the Philippines' strong 2012 growth (6.3% Q1, 5.9% Q2), Panganiban addresses how the judiciary can help the economy. The primary responsibility for economic growth rests with elected leaders and the private sector -- the judiciary's proper role is deferential interpretation: absent a clear constitutional violation or grave abuse of discretion, courts must respect the economic programs of political leaders who are accountable to voters. In human rights cases the rule is reversed: courts strictly construe laws in favor of the people and against the government. He illustrates with two SC cases. Tañada v. Angara (May 2, 1997) unanimously upheld WTO ratification using deferential interpretation -- the Constitution has a bias for Filipino goods but also recognizes globalization, and 'whether such exercise was wise, beneficial or viable is outside the realm of judicial inquiry.' The NAIA Terminal 3 contract was correctly voided because it had a specific, clear violation of public bidding law -- an 'unwanted interloper' objection the SC rebuffed by enforcing the 'level the playing field' axiom. Long-term investors expect stable, consistent, and predictable jurisprudence; courts should interfere only for specific legal defects or GAD, not policy disagreements. The FDR-New Deal parallel warns against obstruction: the US SC's blocking of New Deal programs prompted court-packing plans, averted only when Justice Owen Roberts joined the liberal bloc ('switch in time that saved nine').
